docs.text: HardFOC core library HardFOC Core Drivers ¶ Every HardFOC device driver and the platform layer they run on, collected as git submodules at pinned commits. One repository to add to a project; each driver keeps its own repository, tests and documentation site. Driver catalogue Using the drivers Source on GitHub A product needs a dozen drivers that must agree on one platform interface and move together. hf-core-drivers pins a set of driver commits that build together, plus the two platform repositories they share: the MCU interface layer and the board pin maps. hf-core consumes it and compiles only the drivers a board turns on. One umbrella, one submodule per chip Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Board HALs and products build on hf-core, whose handlers adapt each driver to the platform. hf-core-drivers holds the device drivers under external/ (one per repository, names read from .gitmodules) and the platform layer under internal/. The drivers talk to the chips through interfaces that the platform layer implements for the MCU. Drawn from: .gitmodules submodule paths ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/umbrella.py . What you get ¶ One submodule per chip. Motor controllers, solenoid drivers, encoders, IMUs, ADCs, sensors, expanders, PMIC, EEPROM and secure element. See the driver catalogue . A platform layer. internal/hf-internal-interface-wrap (MCU peripheral interfaces) and internal/hf-pincfg (board pin maps). See Platform layer . Drivers with no platform code. Each driver talks to a small interface class; the board provides it. See How a driver is built . Pinned, reviewed versions. A submodule bump is a pull request here. See Updating submodules . One coding standard. Naming, errors, memory and documentation rules shared by every driver. See Coding standards . Where to go next ¶ Driver catalogue A card per chip with its bus and documentation site. Using the drivers Add the umbrella, turn drivers on in hf-core. Platform layer The interface layer and pin maps every driver builds on. Updating submodules Bump a driver, check it, open the pull request.

docs.text: Coding standards ¶ The naming, error-handling, memory and documentation rules shared by the HardFOC drivers, in brief. The full text, with rationale and examples, is CODING_STANDARDS.md . When a driver's existing code uses a different but consistent style, match the file you are editing. Naming ¶ Element Convention Example Public functions PascalCase Init() , EnableChannel() Private functions camelCase checkInitialized() , transferFrame() Member variables snake_case with trailing _ comm_ , initialized_ Static member variables snake_case with trailing _ instance_count_ Global variables g_ prefix, snake_case g_transfer_count Constants ( constexpr , const ) UPPER_CASE MAX_CHANNELS , CH_CTRL Enum classes PascalCase DriverError , ChannelMode Enum values (errors, states) PascalCase None , NotInitialized Enum values (flags, bits) UPPER_CASE CRC_ERROR Local variables, parameters snake_case current_value , current_ma Type aliases, classes, structs PascalCase CommResult , ChannelConfig , MAX22200 Namespaces lowercase (preferred) max22200 , tmc9660 Macros UPPER_CASE DEVICE_HPP Files lowercase with underscores max22200_spi_interface.hpp Repositories lowercase with dashes hf-max22200-driver Prefer full words ( channel , not ch ) and put units in names ( current_setpoint_ma_ ). Code organisation ¶ Include guards ( #ifndef DEVICE_HPP ), then includes in the order: system headers, third-party headers, the driver's own headers. Classes list public, then protected, then private members; within a section constructors first and data members last. Fixed-width integer types ( uint8_t , int32_t ) for anything that maps to hardware. Errors ¶ C++ drivers return results: std::expected on C++23, or the driver's own expected -style polyfill on C++20. C code returns status codes. Every call that can fail is checked and its error propagated; no silent fallbacks. Memory and threads ¶ Stack and static storage first; RAII for every resource; smart pointers when dynamic allocation is unavoidable. Drivers are not thread-safe by default: the caller synchronises shared access unless a function is documented as thread-safe. Document which functions are thread-safe; protect shared state with std::atomic or a mutex, and prefer class members to globals. Documentation ¶ Doxygen comments ( @brief , @param , @return ) on every public declaration. Inline comments say why, not what. Documentation sites follow the HardFOC documentation style guide .

docs.text: How a driver is built ¶ The shape every HardFOC driver shares, so that a driver written once runs on any MCU the platform supports. Layer Lives in Knows about Driver core external/<driver>/inc , src The chip: registers, commands, timing, units, faults Communication interface external/<driver>/inc The handful of operations the driver needs: transfer, GPIO, delay Platform port hf-core handlers, or your project The MCU, through internal/hf-internal-interface-wrap or the vendor SDK The standard each driver is brought to ¶ No platform code in the driver. No ESP-IDF, STM32 HAL or RTOS includes in the driver core. No exceptions, no heap in the hot path. Results come back as status codes or std::expected -style types. Host tests against a mock of the communication interface, run in CI. ESP32 examples , built in CI from examples/esp32/app_config.yml . A documentation site with the standard page set: Quickstart, Installation, Hardware, Architecture, API guide, Porting, Examples, Testing and CI. Drivers are moved to this standard one by one; each driver's Testing and CI page says what it has today. The details (naming, error types, include order, Doxygen comments) are in the coding standards . The pilot for the current documentation and structure is the TMC9660 driver . Next: Driver catalogue .

docs.text: Using the drivers ¶ Add the umbrella to a project and build the drivers a board needs, through hf-core or on their own. Through hf-core ¶ hf-core carries this repository as its hf-core-drivers submodule and compiles a driver only when its switch is on. A board HAL sets the switches and includes the build settings: set ( HF_CORE_MCU "ESP32" ) set ( HF_CORE_RTOS "FREERTOS" ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_TMC9660 ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_PCAL95555 ON ) set ( HF_CORE_ENABLE_NTC_THERMISTOR ON ) include ( path/to/hf-core/cmake/hf_core_build_settings.cmake ) # Outputs: HF_CORE_SOURCES, HF_CORE_INCLUDE_DIRS, HF_CORE_COMPILE_DEFINITIONS, HF_CORE_IDF_REQUIRES For each enabled driver, hf_core_build_settings.cmake includes that driver's own external/<driver>/cmake/hf_<name>_build_settings.cmake , and adds the platform layer from internal/ . Clone recursively, or initialise the submodules a board uses: git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-core.git The switches and their defaults are documented on the hf-core site . On their own ¶ Every driver is a standalone repository with a CMake target and an ESP-IDF component; use it directly when you do not need hf-core: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-tmc9660-driver.git external/hf-tmc9660-driver Each driver's Installation page lists its target, options and ESP-IDF component. Start from the driver catalogue . The umbrella on its own ¶ git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-core-drivers.git hf-core-drivers git -C hf-core-drivers submodule update --init --depth 1 external/hf-tmc9660-driver internal/hf-pincfg The umbrella has no build files of its own: it pins versions. Initialise only the submodules you build. Next: Platform layer .

docs.text: Platform layer ¶ The two repositories under internal/ that every driver and board HAL builds on. Path What it is Documentation internal/hf-internal-interface-wrap Hardware-agnostic base classes for MCU peripherals (GPIO, ADC, I²C, SPI, UART, CAN, PWM, NVS, timers and more) with ESP32 implementations Site · GitHub internal/hf-pincfg Compile-time functional pin maps per board (Vortex V1, Flux V1) as X-macro rows Site · GitHub How they fit together ¶ A driver in external/ depends on neither: it defines its own small communication interface (a CRTP class or a few virtual methods) and never includes an MCU header. hf-core handlers implement each driver's interface on top of the Base* classes of the interface layer, so one adapter serves every MCU the interface layer supports. A board HAL selects its pin map with one HARDFOC_BOARD_* define and registers GPIO and ADC channels from it. Porting to a new MCU means implementing the interface layer's Base* classes for it; the drivers do not change. Next: Updating submodules .

docs.text: Updating submodules ¶ Move a driver to a newer commit, check it and open the pull request that pins it. Merge the change in the driver's repository first. The umbrella only ever points at commits on a driver's main . Bump the pointer here. git switch -c bump/hf-tmc9660-driver git submodule update --init external/hf-tmc9660-driver git -C external/hf-tmc9660-driver fetch origin main git -C external/hf-tmc9660-driver checkout origin/main git add external/hf-tmc9660-driver git commit -m "Bump hf-tmc9660-driver for <the change>" Build it where it is used. Point hf-core's hf-core-drivers submodule at your branch and run its host build and the ESP32 examples of the boards that enable the driver. Open the pull request here, naming the driver change it brings in. After the merge, bump hf-core-drivers in hf-core. Adding a driver ¶ git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/<repo>.git external/<repo> . Add an entry for it to tools/docs/drivers.yml : group, chip, vendor, function, bus, language and whether it has a documentation site. Check each fact against the driver's README. Run hardfoc-docs gen and mkdocs build --strict ; the catalogue gains a card. Checking where every submodule points ¶ git submodule status # commit of each submodule; a leading '-' means not initialised git submodule foreach --quiet 'echo "$name $(git describe --tags --always)"' Next: Coding standards .

docs.text: Move a driver to a newer commit, check it and open the pull request that pins it. Merge the change in the driver's repository first. The umbrella only ever points at commits on a driver's main . Bump the pointer here. git switch -c bump/hf-tmc9660-driver git submodule update --init external/hf-tmc9660-driver git -C external/hf-tmc9660-driver fetch origin main git -C external/hf-tmc9660-driver checkout origin/main git add external/hf-tmc9660-driver git commit -m "Bump hf-tmc9660-driver for <the change>" Build it where it is used. Point hf-core's hf-core-drivers submodule at your branch and run its host build and the ESP32 examples of the boards that enable the driver. Open the pull request here, naming the driver change it brings in. After the merge, bump hf-core-drivers in hf-core.

Add an entry for it to tools/docs/drivers.yml : group, chip, vendor, function, bus, language and whether it has a documentation site. Check each fact against the driver's README. Run hardfoc-docs gen and mkdocs build --strict ; the catalogue gains a card.

docs.text: Figures ¶ Every figure on this site is drawn by a Python module from facts extracted from the code, so it is rebuilt, not redrawn, when the code changes. CI runs hardfoc-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. One umbrella, one submodule per chip ¶ One umbrella, one submodule per chip Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Board HALs and products build on hf-core, whose handlers adapt each driver to the platform. hf-core-drivers holds the device drivers under external/ (one per repository, names read from .gitmodules) and the platform layer under internal/. The drivers talk to the chips through interfaces that the platform layer implements for the MCU. Drawn from: .gitmodules submodule paths ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/umbrella.py .
